title: Grade 7 Revision Lab
tagline: Build confidence with varied practice, clear explanations and a fresh timed challenge.

topics.title: Flowchart symbols and tracing
topics.summary: Use the symbol’s job to identify its shape, then follow arrows and keep track of the current stored value.
tips: Oval: Start or Stop. Rectangle: a process or calculation. Diamond: a decision. Parallelogram: input or output.
In a trace, evaluate the right-hand side using the current value before storing the new value.
Record a value after the stated instruction has run, not before it.

topics.title: Outputs, errors and flowcharts
topics.summary: Output displays the latest stored value. A complete flowchart has a connected route through its instructions.
tips: Trace the program before predicting what it displays; printing a value does not change it.
Check that an update uses the current variable when it is supposed to increase or decrease it.
Include Start and Stop, suitable symbols, directional arrows and clearly labelled decision routes.

topics.title: Decisions and comparisons
topics.summary: Turn words such as below, at least and at most into comparisons, paying attention to whether the boundary is included.
tips: Below uses <, and above uses >. At least uses >=, and at most uses <=.
Test a boundary value to check whether equality is handled correctly.
A decision has two possible truth results. Make the Yes and No routes match the condition you wrote.

topics.title: Boolean logic: AND, OR, NOT
topics.summary: Evaluate comparisons first, then combine or reverse their truth values using the stated operator.
tips: AND is True only when both inputs are True.
OR is True when at least one input is True, including when both are True.
NOT reverses one truth value. Keep independent expressions separate rather than carrying one answer into the next.

topics.title: Patterns and subroutines
topics.summary: A subroutine gives a reusable group of instructions a name so that the main program can call it.
tips: Find the smallest complete action block that repeats, preserving the action order.
A shared definition reduces repeated copies. Explain the effect: one change can apply to every call.
After a subroutine returns, the main program continues just after the call.

topics.title: Tracing and debugging subroutines
topics.summary: Debugging means finding and correcting errors. Trace every action in each complete subroutine call.
tips: Count how many times the subroutine is called and what happens during one call.
The final action of the last call determines the final state of a light or other stored state.
Setting a variable to a fixed number is different from adding that number to its current value.

topics.title: Python syntax, IDE and print
topics.summary: Syntax is the set of rules for writing valid Python statements. An IDE helps you edit, run and debug them.
tips: Check matching quotation marks and parentheses when repairing a print statement.
print("Hello") displays Hello. The surrounding quotes are part of the code, not the displayed text.
print(name) displays the stored value; print("name") displays the word name.

topics.title: Variables, assignment and arithmetic
topics.summary: An assignment evaluates the right side and stores its result in the variable named on the left.
tips: Use * for multiplication in Python. Replace variable names with their current values when tracing an expression.
A single = performs assignment in Python; it is not a question asking whether two values are equal.
If a question requests a calculation, include the expression rather than replacing it with only the final number.

topics.title: Updates and data types
topics.summary: An update can use a variable’s old value to calculate its new one. Data types describe the kind of value being stored.
tips: In score = score + 2, calculate from the old score and then replace the stored value.
Whole-number literals such as 18 are integers; decimal literals such as 12.5 are floats.
Quoted values are strings, even if their characters look like digits. True and False without quotes are Boolean values.

topics.title: User input
topics.summary: input() reads text entered by the user. An assignment can store that response in a named variable.
tips: The text inside input’s parentheses is the prompt displayed before the user types.
The entered response, rather than the prompt, is what input returns for the assignment to store.
Use the variable without quotation marks when displaying the stored response.

context.text: A robot performs these four actions in order.

parts.prompt: Write the two-action pattern that repeats.
parts.hint: Compare the first pair of actions with the second pair, keeping their order.

steps.title: Match the repeated actions
steps.text: Steps 1 and 3 match, and steps 2 and 4 match. This shows that a two-action block is repeated.

steps.title: Retain the sequence
steps.text: The block begins with Play a tone and then Turn clockwise. Reversing the order would change the robot’s behaviour.

parts.model: Play a tone, then turn clockwise.
rubric: Play a tone followed by turn clockwise (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Complete the table for this separate program.

blocks.text: The lamp starts OFF. The subroutine Flash turns the lamp ON, displays one star, and turns the lamp OFF. The main program calls Flash three times.

parts.hint: Work out the effect of one whole call, then apply the stated number of calls.

steps.title: Trace one complete call
steps.text: Each Flash call displays one star and finishes by turning the lamp OFF.

steps.title: Count calls and check the last action
steps.text: Three complete calls display three stars. The third call also ends with the lamp OFF, so repeated calls do not leave it ON.

parts.model: Three stars are displayed. The lamp finishes OFF.
rubric: 3 stars (1 mark).
Final lamp state OFF (1 mark).

parts.prompt: For this part only, is_wet is False and has_umbrella is True. Complete the table with True or False.
parts.hint: Use the supplied truth values separately in each row. Do not carry a result from one row into another.

steps.title: Evaluate OR
steps.text: is_wet OR has_umbrella becomes False OR True. OR needs at least one True value, so this expression is True.

steps.title: Evaluate NOT independently
steps.text: has_umbrella is True. NOT reverses that value, making NOT has_umbrella False.

parts.model: True; False, in row order.
rubric: OR expression is True (1 mark).
NOT expression is False (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Which Python value has a Boolean data type?
parts.hint: Look carefully at both the spelling and the quotation marks around each option.

steps.title: Recognise the Boolean literals
steps.text: Python uses True and False, with capital first letters, as Boolean values. They have no surrounding quotation marks.

steps.title: Check the other forms
steps.text: False is Boolean. "False" is text because it is quoted, 0 is an integer, and 0.0 is a float.

parts.model:
A. False
False is a Boolean literal; quotation marks would make it a string.
rubric: A — False (1 mark).

context.text: The four checks are independent. Use the values and instructions stated in each part.

parts.prompt: State the value output after these flowchart instructions run in order.
parts.hint: Use the current stored value when the update runs, then read that value at OUTPUT.

steps.title: Store and update the value
steps.text: The first instruction stores 17. The next instruction adds 4 to that stored value.

steps.title: Read the output instruction
steps.text: OUTPUT displays the updated seedlings value. It does not return to the starting value or change it again.

parts.model: 21. The update stores 17 + 4, and OUTPUT displays the new value.
rubric: [1] Output 21.

parts.prompt: plants is a whole number. Write a comparison that is True when plants is at least 11.
parts.hint: The comparison must include 11 itself and every larger whole number.

steps.title: Translate the inclusive lower limit
steps.text: At least means greater than or equal to the stated boundary.

steps.title: Check values beside the boundary
steps.text: The condition is false for 10 and true for 11. Because plants is a whole-number count, plants > 10 gives the same result.

parts.model: plants >= 11
rubric: [1] plants >= 11 or an equivalent whole-number comparison, including plants > 10 or 11 <= plants.

parts.prompt: is_dry is True and has_water is False. State the result of is_dry AND has_water.
parts.hint: AND requires both conditions to be true.

steps.title: Substitute the two truth values
steps.text: The expression becomes True AND False. The second required condition is not satisfied.

steps.title: Apply the AND rule
steps.text: AND is true only when both sides are true. With one false side, the result is False.

parts.model: False. Both conditions are required, but has_water is False.
rubric: [1] False.

parts.prompt: The subroutine Chime plays one chime and then returns. The main program calls Chime four times. State the number of chimes played.
parts.hint: Count what one call does, then account for every call.

steps.title: Trace one call
steps.text: Each call runs the subroutine once and produces one chime before returning.

steps.title: Combine the repeated calls
steps.text: Four separate calls produce four chimes in total. Returning does not stop the main program from making the next call.

parts.model: 4 chimes.
rubric: [1] 4 chimes.

parts.prompt: A decision must be True when temperature is below 10. Which comparison is correct?
parts.hint: Test what should happen when temperature is exactly 10 before choosing an operator.

steps.title: Read the boundary word
steps.text: Below means strictly smaller. A temperature equal to 10 must not satisfy the decision.

steps.title: Use the strict comparison
steps.text: temperature < 10 is True for values smaller than 10 and False for 10 itself. Using <= would incorrectly include the boundary.

parts.model:
B. temperature < 10
The < operator means strictly less than; 10 itself is excluded.
rubric: B — temperature < 10 (1 mark).

parts.prompt: State the output of this Python program.
parts.hint: Evaluate the expression on the right of = before reading the print statement.

steps.title: Calculate and store
steps.text: The expression 6 + 4 has the value 10. The assignment stores that result in total.

steps.title: Display the variable value
steps.text: print(total) displays the value stored in total, not the variable name. The output is 10.

parts.prompt: Write one Python assignment that calculates 5 multiplied by 3 and stores the result in total_cost.
parts.hint: Put the destination variable on the left and use Python’s multiplication operator on the right.

widgets.label: Choose an assignment that performs the requested calculation

steps.title: Build the calculation
steps.text: Python uses * for multiplication, so the requested expression is 5 * 3. Reversing the two factors would give the same product.

steps.title: Store the result in the named variable
steps.text: Write total_cost on the left of = and the expression on the right. Giving only 15 does not show the requested calculation.

parts.model: total_cost = 5 * 3
rubric: total_cost = 5 * 3 or total_cost = 3 * 5. Accept parentheses. Do not accept only total_cost = 15 because the calculation was requested. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: State what the assignment operator = does in apples_per_box = 4.
parts.hint: Read assignment as an instruction to store a value, rather than as a question about equality.

widgets.label: Choose what = does in this statement

steps.title: Find the source and destination
steps.text: In an assignment, the expression on the right provides the value. The name on the left is the variable that receives it.

steps.title: Apply that rule here
steps.text: The right side is 4 and the destination is apples_per_box, so the statement stores 4 there. It is not an equality test.

parts.model: It stores the value 4 in the variable apples_per_box.
rubric: Stores/assigns the right-hand value in the named variable. Do not accept checks whether the two sides are equal. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: The user types Amina when this statement runs. State the value stored in name.
parts.hint: Distinguish the prompt shown by the program from the text the user actually enters.

widgets.label: Choose the text stored in name

steps.title: Identify the entered response
steps.text: The prompt is Your name:, but the question says the user types Amina. input returns the entered text.

steps.title: Follow the assignment
steps.text: The returned text is stored in name. The stored value is therefore Amina, not the prompt or the variable name.

parts.model: Amina
rubric: Amina. Accept quotation marks around the text. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: State the message displayed before the user types their name.
parts.hint: Look at the text inside input’s parentheses, before the user’s response is read.

widgets.label: Choose the message displayed before the user types

steps.title: Find the prompt argument
steps.text: The string inside input("Your name: ") is the prompt. It is shown before Python waits for the user to type.

steps.title: Separate prompt from response
steps.text: The message is Your name:. Amina is the later response, so it is not the message displayed first.

parts.model: Your name:
rubric: Your name: . Accept omission of the colon or final space; accept quotation marks. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Which Boolean operator changes True to False and False to True?
parts.hint: Look for an operator that works on one truth value rather than combining two.

steps.title: Separate the operator roles
steps.text: AND and OR combine two Boolean values. The reversal operation works on one Boolean value.

steps.title: Apply the reversal rule
steps.text: NOT True is False, and NOT False is True. That is exactly the change described in the question.

parts.model:
A. NOT
NOT reverses a Boolean truth value.
rubric: A — NOT (1 mark).

questions.label: Practice 07
questions.title: Trace and repair a short flowchart

context.text: These instructions run in order in a flowchart. The arrow <- means assign a value.

parts.prompt: Complete the trace table with the value of stars after each stated step.
parts.hint: Store the starting value first, then use it on the right-hand side of the update.

steps.title: Read the first assignment
steps.text: Step 1 assigns 6 to stars. This sets the starting value rather than adding to an earlier value.

steps.title: Apply the update
steps.text: Step 2 uses that stored 6, adds 2 and stores 8 back into stars. The trace entries are 6 and 8.

parts.model: After step 1: 6. After step 2: 8.
rubric: Step 1 is 6 (1 mark).
Step 2 is 8; on paper, allow the stated step 1 value plus 2 (1 mark).

parts.prompt: State the value output at step 3.
parts.hint: Use the value left by the most recent assignment.

steps.title: Find the latest stored value
steps.text: The update has changed stars from 6 to 8. No further assignment occurs before OUTPUT.

steps.title: Read the output instruction
steps.text: OUTPUT stars displays the current stored value, so it displays 8. Output does not change stars.

rubric: 8; on paper, allow the value recorded after step 2 (1 mark).

parts.prompt: For a separate decision, tickets is a whole number. Choose the comparison that is True for 5 or more tickets.
parts.hint: Test the boundary value and one value below it.

steps.title: Include the boundary
steps.text: The phrase 5 or more includes exactly 5 as well as larger whole numbers.

steps.title: Use an inclusive lower limit
steps.text: tickets >= 5 includes all required values. tickets > 5 would exclude 5, while an equality check would exclude numbers above 5.

parts.model: tickets >= 5. For a whole-number input, tickets > 4 is also equivalent.
rubric: Select tickets >= 5; accept a clearly equivalent comparison when practising on paper (1 mark).

parts.prompt: A different process should add 2 to stars, but it contains stars <- 2. Write the corrected instruction.
parts.hint: The new value must depend on the existing value, not just a fixed number.

steps.title: Identify why the original fails
steps.text: stars <- 2 stores the fixed value 2. It does not use the old value, so it cannot add 2 to it.

steps.title: Calculate from the old value
steps.text: stars + 2 uses the current value and increases it by 2. Store that result back into stars.

parts.model: stars <- stars + 2
rubric: stars <- stars + 2, or a clearly equivalent assignment such as stars = stars + 2 (1 mark).

parts.prompt: What is a subroutine?
parts.hint: Think about something a program can call and then return from.

widgets.label: Choose one answer
options: A named collection of values stored in a program.
A named comment explaining how a program works.
A named group of instructions that can be called when needed.
A named instruction that always ends the whole program.

steps.title: Identify what is reusable
steps.text: A subroutine holds a group of instructions under a name. The instructions can run whenever the program calls that name.

steps.title: Distinguish instructions from data
steps.text: A collection of values stores data, and a comment explains code. Neither describes a named group of callable instructions, so the third option is correct.

parts.model:
C. A named group of instructions that can be called when needed.
A subroutine is a named group of reusable instructions that can be called from elsewhere in a program.
rubric: C — A named group of instructions that can be called when needed. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: A box may hold at most 12 items. Which comparison is True when the number items is allowed?
parts.hint: Check whether a box containing exactly 12 items should be allowed.

steps.title: Interpret the boundary
steps.text: At most 12 means 12 or fewer. The boundary value 12 must be included.

steps.title: Choose the inclusive comparison
steps.text: items <= 12 is True below the limit and at the limit. The strict < comparison would wrongly reject exactly 12.

parts.model: B. items <= 12.
rubric: B — items <= 12 (1 mark).

parts.prompt: An algorithm sets value to 4, adds 3 to value, then outputs value. What is output?
parts.hint: Follow the instructions in order, and keep the updated value for the output.

steps.title: Store the starting value
steps.text: The first instruction stores 4 in value. This is the number used by the next instruction.

steps.title: Update, then display
steps.text: Adding 3 replaces the stored value with 4 + 3 = 7. The output instruction displays this latest value, so the answer is 7.

parts.model:
D. 7
The value changes from 4 to 4 + 3, which is 7.
rubric: D — 7 (1 mark).

parts.prompt: What is meant by the syntax of a programming language?
parts.hint: Consider why a statement might be rejected before it can run.

widgets.label: Choose one answer
options: The final value output by a program.
The hardware used to run a program.
The time taken to run a program.
The rules for writing valid statements in that language.

steps.title: Look at statement rules
steps.text: A language needs rules for how instructions are written, including spelling, punctuation and structure. These rules are its syntax.

steps.title: Separate syntax from results
steps.text: Output and running time describe what happens during execution. Hardware is the equipment. None of these is the set of rules for writing valid statements.

parts.model:
D. The rules for writing valid statements in that language.
Syntax defines the permitted structure and spelling of statements.
rubric: D — The rules for writing valid statements in that language. (1 mark).

context.text: A visitor buys two badges that cost 4 each. The program must read the visitor's name, calculate the badge cost by multiplying 2 and 4, and then add a bag fee of 1 to total. It must display the entered name, followed by the final total on the next line.

parts.prompt: Complete the five blanks in the Python 3 program.
parts.hint: Match each blank to one requirement: read text, calculate a product, update a total, then display two variable values.

widgets.label: Blank 1: expression that reads the visitor’s name

steps.title: Read text into name
steps.text: input("Name: ") reads the visitor’s typed name. The supplied name = stores that text, while print would only display a message.

steps.title: Show the requested multiplication
steps.text: Two badges at 4 each cost 2 * 4 = 8. Put the multiplication in the blank because the question asks the program to calculate it.

steps.title: Update the existing total
steps.text: The third line already says total = total +. Adding 1 changes the stored total from 8 to 9.

steps.title: Print values in the requested order
steps.text: Use name inside the first print and total inside the second. Quoting either identifier would display the word itself instead of its stored value.

parts.model:
name = input("Name: ")
total = 2 * 4
total = total + 1
print(name)
print(total)
rubric: First blank: input("Name: ") or input() with any suitable optional prompt. The entered text is stored in name. (1 mark).
Second blank: 2 * 4 or 4 * 2. Accept parentheses. The question requests a calculation, so do not accept only 8. (1 mark).
Third blank: 1. The supplied statement then updates total to include the bag fee. (1 mark).
Fourth blank: name, without quotation marks, so the program displays the entered text. (1 mark).
Fifth blank: total, without quotation marks, so the program displays the calculated final value. Award independently of an earlier calculation error. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: What does this Python program output?
parts.hint: Find the current value of each variable, then use the operator inside print().

steps.title: Read both assignments
steps.text: packs stores 3 and items_per_pack stores 4. Use these stored numbers when evaluating the expression.

steps.title: Apply multiplication
steps.text: The * operator multiplies. The expression is 3 * 4 = 12, and print displays 12. Adding would give a different result.

parts.model:
B. 12
The multiplication operator gives 3 times 4, which is 12.
rubric: B — 12 (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Which flowchart symbol should contain the instruction coins <- coins + 1?
parts.hint: Decide whether the instruction reads data, asks a question, or changes a stored value.

steps.title: Identify the action
steps.text: coins <- coins + 1 calculates a new value and stores it. This is a process, not an input, output or decision.

steps.title: Match the action to the shape
steps.text: A rectangle represents a process. The instruction should therefore go inside a rectangle.

parts.model: C. Rectangle. The instruction calculates and stores a value, so it is a process.
rubric: C — Rectangle (1 mark).

parts.prompt: What does this Python statement display?
parts.hint: Separate Python’s punctuation from the text that reaches the screen.

steps.title: Identify the string content
steps.text: The string inside the quotation marks is Start, with a capital S.

steps.title: Apply print
steps.text: print displays the content of the string, so it displays Start without quotation marks or the surrounding Python statement.

parts.model: C. Start.
rubric: C — Start (1 mark).

parts.prompt: What is the data type of the Python value 18?
parts.hint: Check whether the value has a decimal point, quotation marks, or a Boolean name.

steps.title: Inspect the written value
steps.text: 18 is an unquoted whole-number literal. There is no decimal point and it is not True or False.

steps.title: Choose the matching type
steps.text: Python stores this literal as an integer. Quotation marks would make a text value, and a decimal point such as 18.0 would indicate a float.

parts.model: A. Integer.
rubric: A — Integer (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Which flowchart symbol is normally used for Start and Stop?
parts.hint: Think about the symbol that marks an endpoint, rather than an action or a decision.

steps.title: Identify the role
steps.text: Start and Stop mark where an algorithm begins and finishes. They do not calculate a value, receive data or choose a branch.

steps.title: Match the standard symbol
steps.text: An oval is a terminator symbol used for these endpoints. A rectangle is a process, a parallelogram is input/output and a diamond is a decision.

parts.model: C. Oval. Start and Stop use terminator symbols.
rubric: [1] Select C: Oval

parts.prompt: State one task an integrated development environment (IDE) helps a programmer carry out.
parts.hint: Think about a tool that helps a person write, run or inspect code.

widgets.label: Choose a valid IDE task
options: Guarantee that a program has no logic errors
Choose the problem requirements without the programmer

steps.title: Identify what an IDE provides
steps.text: An integrated development environment brings programming tools together. An editor and a way to run code are typical examples.

steps.title: Give an actual task
steps.text: Editing and running code is a valid task. An IDE can help find problems, but it does not guarantee correct logic or decide the problem requirements.

parts.model: Edit, run or debug a program.
rubric: Any one valid IDE task: writing/editing code, running a program, debugging, showing syntax errors, or displaying program output. Do not accept only typing the expansion of IDE. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Rewrite the line to correct its syntax error.
parts.hint: Check that the quotation marks form a matching pair and that print has its closing parenthesis.

steps.title: Locate the unfinished string
steps.text: The opening double quote starts the text Ready. The original line has no matching closing quote before the parenthesis.

steps.title: Close the string and call
steps.text: Put the matching quotation mark after Ready and retain the closing parenthesis. Either matching single or matching double quotation marks is valid.

parts.model: print("Ready")
rubric: print("Ready") or print('Ready') with matching quotation marks and closing parenthesis. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: State exactly what this Python statement displays.
parts.hint: Separate the text inside the quotation marks from the punctuation used to write the Python statement.

steps.title: Identify the string content
steps.text: The quotation marks tell Python where the text begins and ends. The text inside them is Welcome, including the capital W.

steps.title: Display only the content
steps.text: print displays the string content. It does not display the quotation marks or the word print, so the output is Welcome.

parts.model: Welcome
rubric: Welcome, without quotation marks. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: State the data type of each value.
parts.hint: Check whether each value is a decimal number or text surrounded by quotation marks.

steps.title: Classify the unquoted decimal
steps.text: 12.5 is a numeric value with a decimal point, so its Python data type is float. The school answer real is also accepted.

steps.title: Classify the quoted value
steps.text: "Hello" is surrounded by quotation marks, so it is a string. The word inside the quotes is text, not a Boolean value or a number.

parts.model: 12.5: float or real. "Hello": string.
rubric: 12.5 is float; accept real. (1 mark).
"Hello" is string; accept str. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Which shortest block can be repeated to create the entire sequence shown?

blocks.text: Clap → Tap → Tap → Clap → Tap → Tap

parts.hint: Start with the first action and check that repeating a proposed block recreates every action in the same order.

steps.title: Check the first complete block
steps.text: The first three actions are Clap, Tap, Tap. The next three actions match that block exactly.

steps.title: Check that a shorter block does not work
steps.text: Repeating Clap, Tap would put Clap in position 3, but position 3 is Tap. A three-action block is needed to reproduce all six actions.
steps.code: Clap, Tap, Tap | Clap, Tap, Tap

parts.model: C. Clap, Tap, Tap. Repeating that block twice recreates the six actions.
rubric: [1] Select C: Clap, Tap, Tap

parts.prompt: Which Python statement asks the user for a name and stores the answer in name?
parts.hint: Look for both a function call and an assignment to the requested variable.

steps.title: Read the entered text
steps.text: input("Name: ") displays a prompt, waits for the user, and returns the text entered. The parentheses are needed to call input.

steps.title: Store the response
steps.text: Putting name = before the call stores the returned text in name. print only displays something, and assigning "Name: " only stores that fixed text.

parts.model:
D. name = input("Name: ")
input("Name: ") asks for text and the assignment stores the entered text in name.
rubric: D — name = input("Name: ") (1 mark).

context.text: A club buys three notebooks at 2 each and two pens at 1 each. The program must read the club name, calculate the notebook cost in total by multiplying 3 and 2, calculate the pen cost in pen_cost by multiplying 2 and 1, and add pen_cost to total. It must display the entered club name, followed by the final total on the next line.

parts.prompt: Complete the five blanks in the Python 3 program.
parts.hint: Work through the requirements in order. The update must include both the old total and the pen cost.

widgets.label: Blank 4: expression for the updated total
Blank 5: value displayed after the club name

steps.title: Read the club name as text
steps.text: input("Club: ") reads the typed name, and the supplied assignment stores it in club. A suitable optional prompt may also be used in a paper solution.

steps.title: Calculate the two costs
steps.text: The notebooks cost 3 * 2 = 6 and the pens cost 2 * 1 = 2. Keep the multiplications in the blanks because the program is required to calculate them.

steps.title: Update the stored total
steps.text: total + pen_cost adds the pen cost to the existing notebook cost. The assignment replaces total with 6 + 2 = 8.

steps.title: Display the requested results
steps.text: print(club) is already supplied. The last blank needs total without quotes, so the final numeric value appears on the next line.

parts.model:
club = input("Club: ")
total = 3 * 2
pen_cost = 2 * 1
total = total + pen_cost
print(club)
print(total)

If the user enters Chess, the two result lines are:
Chess
8
rubric: Blank 1: input("Club: ") or input() with any suitable optional prompt (1 mark).
Blank 2: 3 * 2 or 2 * 3, with optional parentheses; do not accept only 6 because a calculation is required (1 mark).
Blank 3: 2 * 1 or 1 * 2, with optional parentheses; do not accept only 2 because a calculation is required (1 mark).
Blank 4: total + pen_cost or pen_cost + total. Award the update independently of an earlier arithmetic error (1 mark).
Blank 5: total without quotation marks, so the program displays its stored value. Award independently of previous errors (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Which flowchart symbol is used for input or output?
parts.hint: Think about whether information is entering, leaving or being processed by the program.

steps.title: Match the job to a symbol
steps.text: Flowcharts use different shapes for different jobs: a process changes a value, a decision asks a question, and an input or output transfers information.

steps.title: Choose the information symbol
steps.text: A parallelogram represents input or output. A rectangle is a process, an oval is a terminator, and a diamond is a decision.

parts.model:
C. Parallelogram
A parallelogram represents an input or output operation.
rubric: C — Parallelogram (1 mark).

context.text: Each short Python snippet is independent of the others.

parts.prompt: The user types Orion when this statement runs. State the value stored in team.
parts.hint: Separate the prompt shown by the program from the response entered by the user.

steps.title: Read the prompt
steps.text: The text Team: asks the user for a response. It is not automatically the response stored in the variable.

steps.title: Follow the assignment

context.text: The main program sets score to 2, calls AddBadge once, outputs score, and then ends. AddBadge should add 2 to the current score. Its faulty flowchart is shown.

parts.prompt: Explain the fault in the process box and write the instruction that adds 2 to score.
parts.hint: Compare setting a fixed value with calculating from the current value. The correction must retain the old score in its calculation.

widgets.label: Choose the explanation of the fault
options: The instruction always sets score to 2 instead of adding 2
The instruction outputs score instead of storing it

steps.title: Explain the fixed assignment
steps.text: score <- 2 replaces the current score with 2 every time. It does not use the previous score, so it cannot increase that score by 2.

steps.title: Use the old value in the update
steps.text: The right side must calculate the current score plus 2 before storing the result back in score.

parts.model: The instruction sets score to 2 instead of adding 2 to its current value. Replace it with score <- score + 2.
rubric: Explains that score is set/reset to 2 rather than increased by 2. (1 mark).
Corrects the process to score <- score + 2; accept score = score + 2 or score += 2 if the meaning is clear. Award independently of the explanation. (1 mark).

steps.title: Apply one call
steps.text: The main program calls the subroutine once, so score changes from 2 to 2 + 2 = 4. There is no second call to add another 2.

rubric: 4. Use the stated corrected behaviour independently of the answer to part a. (1 mark).

context.text: A drinks dispenser reads a whole number called cups. When cups is at least 3, it outputs "Group order". Otherwise, it outputs "Small order". The program then ends.

steps.text: Use an oval for Start, then a parallelogram for INPUT cups. Reading the value must happen before the decision uses it.

steps.title: Test the stated boundary
steps.text: At least 3 includes 3, so cups >= 3 is a suitable decision. For the stated whole-number input, cups > 2 is equivalent. Put the comparison in a decision diamond.

steps.title: Route the two possible results
steps.text: For this guided construction, Yes goes to OUTPUT "Group order" and No goes to OUTPUT "Small order". Both messages belong in output parallelograms.

steps.title: Complete the flow
steps.text: Connect both output routes to a Stop oval with directional arrows. A paper solution may use an inverse condition if its branch destinations are also reversed, as the full rubric explains.

parts.model: Start -> INPUT cups -> decision cups >= 3. The Yes/True branch leads to OUTPUT "Group order"; the No/False branch leads to OUTPUT "Small order". Both branches lead to Stop. Use terminators for Start and Stop, parallelograms for input and outputs, a diamond for the decision and directional arrows.
rubric: Includes Start and Stop terminators and a complete directional route from Start to Stop; allow two separate Stop terminators. (1 mark).
Reads cups using an input parallelogram. (1 mark).
Uses a decision diamond containing cups >= 3 or an equivalent comparison, such as cups > 2 for the stated whole-number input. (1 mark).
Labels the two decision routes Yes/No or True/False and routes them to the appropriate outputs. If the candidate uses the inverse comparison, allow inverted branch destinations. (1 mark).
Includes both exact messages in output parallelograms. Assess correct route placement under the preceding routing mark, so an otherwise correct output is not penalised twice. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: What does debugging a program mean?
parts.hint: Think about the work done after a test reveals a problem in a program.

widgets.label: Choose one answer
options: Writing the first draft of a program.
Finding and correcting errors in a program.
Adding comments to explain a program.
Saving a program with a new filename.

steps.title: Recognise the purpose
steps.text: A program may have an error in its syntax or in what its instructions do. Debugging is the work of finding the cause.

steps.title: Include the repair
steps.text: Debugging also involves correcting the error and checking the change. Writing comments or saving a new filename does not itself fix a fault.

parts.model:
B. Finding and correcting errors in a program.
Debugging means locating and correcting errors.
rubric: B — Finding and correcting errors in a program. (1 mark).

steps.text: Steps 1 and 3 both say Move forward. Steps 2 and 4 both say Flash a light, so the same two-action block appears twice.

steps.text: The pattern begins with Move forward and then Flash a light. Reversing the two actions would describe a different sequence.

rubric: Move forward followed by flash a light. Accept steps 1 to 2 or 3 to 4. (1 mark).

parts.prompt: Explain one benefit of putting the repeated sequence in a subroutine.
parts.hint: Choose one benefit, then explain how calling a shared set of instructions produces that benefit.

widgets.label: Choose the benefit to explain
options: Each call creates a separate copy that must be edited
The repeated instructions can be stored in one shared place
The repeated actions only happen on the first call

widgets.label: Choose the explanation of that benefit
options: The program stops after the first call
Every call keeps the old instructions forever
One change to the shared instructions applies to every call

steps.title: Identify the shared definition
steps.text: A subroutine stores the repeated instructions once. The main program uses its name whenever those instructions are needed.

steps.title: Explain the maintenance effect
steps.text: A change to that one definition is used by every later call. This avoids finding and editing separate copies, which explains the maintenance benefit.

parts.model: The instructions are stored once, so a change to that subroutine updates every place where it is called.
rubric: Identifies a valid benefit, such as reduced duplication, easier maintenance or clearer main program. (1 mark).

Explains the benefit: for example, a change is made once and applies to every call, or the descriptive call makes the main program easier to follow. Do not award both marks for two unexplained benefits. (1 mark).
